clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia caused by heterozygous variants in KIF5A, which encodes a neuronal kinesin motor driving anterograde axonal transport
Presents as either a pure spastic paraparesis or a complicated form with distal amyotrophy, peripheral neuropathy or mild cognitive change
Onset is usually in childhood or early adulthood, with slowly progressive gait spasticity and brisk lower-limb reflexes
KIF5A is allelic with axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 and with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, so family histories can appear phenotypically mixed
Wasting of intrinsic hand and foot muscles, when present, reflects the length-dependent motor axonopathy
Nerve conduction studies help separate pure from complicated disease and identify an associated axonal neuropathy
Care is symptomatic, centring on physiotherapy, spasticity management and orthoses to maintain mobility
reference.pathophysiology: SPG10 results from dominant variants in KIF5A, the gene for a heavy chain of kinesin-1, the principal motor that carries cargo (mitochondria, vesicles and cytoskeletal components) along microtubules towards the axon terminal. Pathogenic changes, often clustered in the motor domain, impair this anterograde transport and disturb cargo delivery to the distal axon. The longest corticospinal and peripheral motor axons are most vulnerable, producing a length-dependent degeneration that manifests as spasticity and, in complicated cases, distal wasting and neuropathy. Distinct variants elsewhere in the gene underlie related Charcot-Marie-Tooth and motor neurone phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegias (SPG4, SPG3A, SPG31)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and juvenile primary lateral sclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Targeted KIF5A sequencing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia or motor neuropathy gene panel
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to define associated neuropathy or amyotrophy
MRI of brain and spine to exclude structural and demyelinating causes
Detailed three-generation family history given variable allelic phenotypes
Cognitive screening where a complicated presentation is suspected
Very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude adrenomyeloneuropathy
redFlags: Prominent lower motor neurone signs or bulbar features suggesting evolution towards a motor neurone disease phenotype
Rapidly progressive weakness that is atypical for slowly progressive hereditary spastic paraplegia
A clear sensory level or sphincter crisis pointing to compressive myelopathy
Early severe cognitive decline warranting broader neurogenetic evaluation
reference.prognosis: Pure SPG10 tends to progress slowly with preserved ambulation for many years, whereas complicated forms with neuropathy or amyotrophy, and families overlapping with motor neurone disease, may follow a more disabling course.
pitfalls: Labelling a case as pure HSP without nerve conduction studies that would reveal an axonal neuropathy
Overlooking the link to Charcot-Marie-Tooth and motor neurone disease when counselling families
Assuming a negative SPG4 test excludes a genetic cause and stopping the panel prematurely
Misreading distal wasting as an unrelated entrapment neuropathy
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
